title: IPO deal walk
description: Six multiple-choice stages following an initial public offering.

concepts.name: IPO process
concepts.summary: The steps a private company follows to sell shares to the public for the first time and list them on an exchange.

concepts.name: Lead underwriter
concepts.summary: The bank that leads an offering: it advises on structure, valuation and timing, runs the process and sells the shares to investors.

concepts.name: Registration statement
concepts.summary: The filing with the securities regulator (Form S-1 in the US) that describes the company and the offering, including a prospectus.

concepts.name: Bookbuilding
concepts.summary: Collecting investor orders at different prices during marketing so the banks can judge demand and set the offer price.

concepts.name: Oversubscription
concepts.summary: Demand for the shares in an offering exceeding the number of shares available.

concepts.name: Greenshoe
concepts.summary: An over-allotment option letting underwriters sell extra shares, commonly up to 15% of the base deal, and support the price after listing.

multipleChoice.title: Role of the lead underwriter
multipleChoice.prompt: A company is preparing an IPO and picks a lead underwriter. Which statement best describes that bank's role?

options.text: It becomes the company's main long-term shareholder
It advises on structure, valuation and timing, leads the process and sells the shares to investors
It only prints and distributes the prospectus
It sets the company's business strategy after listing

explanation: The lead underwriter advises on how to structure the offering, helps decide valuation and timing, runs the execution and places the shares with investors.
It is not intended to be a long-term owner, and its role is not limited to printing documents or setting strategy.

multipleChoice.title: Why diligence matters
multipleChoice.prompt: The banks and their lawyers carry out due diligence while the offering documents are drafted. Why is thorough diligence important to the underwriters?

options.text: It sets the final share price
It guarantees the share price will rise after listing
Underwriters can be liable for material misstatements or omissions, so they need a reasonable basis for the disclosure
It is needed to book the roadshow venues

explanation: Underwriters share responsibility for the accuracy of the offering documents. Diligence gives them a reasonable basis to believe the disclosure is complete and not misleading.
It does not set the price, and nothing in the process can guarantee how the shares trade afterwards.

multipleChoice.title: Regulator review
multipleChoice.prompt: In a US IPO the company files a registration statement with the SEC. What typically happens next?

options.text: The SEC sets the offer price
The shares start trading the same day the registration statement is filed
The SEC approves the investment merits of the company
The SEC reviews the filing and sends comments, which the company answers in amendments before it can go effective

explanation: The SEC reviews the disclosure and sends comment letters. The company responds and amends the filing until the review is complete and the registration can go effective.
The SEC does not set the price or judge whether the company is a good investment; it focuses on disclosure.

multipleChoice.title: Marketing the offering
multipleChoice.prompt: Management and the banks meet investors on a roadshow while the bankers build the book. What is the main purpose of building the book?

options.text: To collect investor orders at different prices so the banks can gauge demand and set the final price
To record the company's accounting books for the auditors
To decide which executives will receive bonuses
To submit the registration statement to the SEC

explanation: Bookbuilding records how many shares investors want at various prices. That demand picture helps the banks and the company choose the final offer price and decide how to allocate shares.
It is a marketing and pricing step, not an accounting or filing step.

multipleChoice.title: Pricing night
multipleChoice.prompt: On pricing night the book is heavily oversubscribed. What can the company and the banks do?

options.text: Cancel every order and restart the roadshow
Raise the price or the range and allocate shares selectively among investors
Give every investor exactly the same number of shares
Issue an unlimited number of extra shares automatically

explanation: Strong demand gives room to price at the top of the range or above it, within what the company and banks judge sensible. The banks also choose how to allocate scarce shares, often favouring long-term investors.
There is no rule that every investor gets equal shares, and the number of shares offered is not unlimited.

multipleChoice.title: After pricing
multipleChoice.prompt: Shares start trading and the offering closes a few days later. What does the greenshoe (over-allotment option) allow the underwriters to do?

options.text: Cancel the IPO if the shares fall on the first day
Release company insiders from their lock-up agreements
Sell additional shares, commonly up to 15% of the base deal, and help support the share price after listing
Buy the company's shares at a discount for the bank's own account

explanation: The greenshoe lets the underwriters sell more shares than the base deal. If the price weakens they can buy shares in the market to cover that short position, which helps support the price; if it holds up they exercise the option with the company.
It does not cancel the offering or release lock-ups.

processes.title: IPO process
processes.description: Follow a US-style IPO from choosing underwriters through filing, marketing and pricing to the aftermarket.
